content: Bifidobacterium animalis is a Gram-positive, anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium that resides in the intestines of most mammals, including humans. It is one of the various species of bifidobacteria found in the human large intestine. Historically, Bifidobacterium animalis and Bifidobacterium lactis were classified as two separate species. However, they are now considered to belong to the same species, Bifidobacterium animalis, with two subspecies: Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. animalis and Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis. Despite this reclassification, the older names, B. animalis and B. lactis, are still commonly used on product labels, as this bacterium is frequently utilized as a probiotic. In many cases, it is unclear which subspecies is present in a given product. The strain B. animalis DN-173010 is widely marketed as a probiotic in the product Activia™, produced by the Danone company (known as Dannon in the United States). This strain is also sold under various trade names, such as L. Regularis in Canada, Bifidus Essensis in Germany, the Netherlands, Romania, and Austria, Bifidus Activo in Spain, and Bifidus Actiregularis in Argentina, Chile, Italy, and Russia. These trade names are not scientific but are designed to appear scientific for marketing purposes. The correct scientific name for this strain is Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis DN-173010. Another commonly used strain is marketed as BB-12® (also referred to as Bb12 or Bb-12). This strain is used in products from various manufacturers worldwide, primarily in dairy products but also in dietary supplements such as pills. It is marketed by Chr. Hansen Ltd, a company based in Denmark. Similar to DN-173010, BB-12® is often labeled as either Bifidobacterium animalis or Bifidobacterium lactis, but its true scientific name is Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis. Both strains, DN-173010 and BB-12®, have been extensively studied, and there is a substantial body of literature supporting their efficacy. For example, studies on BB-12® have demonstrated its effects on the intestinal microbiota of preterm infants, its adherence to human intestinal mucus in healthy infants and during rotavirus infection, and its ability to activate transient pro-inflammatory host responses in intestinal epithelial cells after colonization in germ-free rats. Similarly, research on DN-173010 has shown that fermented milk containing this strain can reduce oro-fecal gut transit time in elderly individuals. Additional studies have demonstrated that DN-173010 shortens colonic transit time in healthy women, as evidenced by double-blind, randomized controlled trials. Other research has confirmed its effects on colonic transit time in healthy humans following the consumption of milk fermented with this probiotic strain.
